Rational numbers

Minus five degrees in January, an account at −€30, the Dead Sea about 430 m below sea level: there are numbers below zero. In this chapter you get to know the negative numbers, put them in order on the number line, find the opposite number and the absolute value, sort numbers into number ranges and use the coordinate system with four quadrants.

UNIT 14 LESSONS

1Negative numbers, opposite number and absolute value

A thermometer has a scale above and below zero. The numbers below zero are written with a minus sign: −5 °C is five degrees below zero. If you extend the number ray beyond zero to the left, you get the number line.

To the right of zero are the positive numbers, to the left the negative numbers. Zero is neither positive nor negative. On the number line: further to the right is larger. That is why $-2 > -7$, although 7 is larger than 2.

Two numbers that are the same distance from zero, but on different sides, are called opposite numbers: 4 and −4. The distance of a number from zero is called its absolute value: $|-4| = 4$.

KEY POINT · NUMBER LINE

Ordering: of two numbers, the one further to the right is the larger: $-7 < -2 < 0 < 3$

The opposite number of $a$ is $-a$: the opposite number of 5 is −5, of −5 it is 5, of 0 it is 0

Absolute value $|a|$: distance from zero, never negative: $|5| = |-5| = 5$

Sign: the plus in front of positive numbers is usually left out: $+3 = 3$.

Germany’s lowest point: near Neuendorf-Sachsenbande in Schleswig-Holstein, about 3.4 m below sea level.

INTERACTIVE · THE NUMBER LINE

Move the two numbers. You see which one is larger, their opposite numbers and their absolute values.

EXAMPLE 1 · ORDERING

Put in order of size: $3$; $-1.5$; $-4$; $0$; $\tfrac12$; $-\tfrac12$

From left to right on the number line:

$-4 < -1.5 < -\tfrac12 < 0 < \tfrac12 < 3$

EXAMPLE 2 · TEMPERATURE DIFFERENCE

In the morning the thermometer shows −6 °C, at midday 4 °C. By how many degrees has it got warmer?

From −6 to 0 is 6 degrees, from 0 to 4 another 4 degrees.

10 degrees warmer

a) −7 and 7   b) 12 and 12   c) 2.5 and 2.5   d) 0 and 0

Which integers lie between −4 and 2? Which have an absolute value less than 3?

−3, −2, −1, 0, 1. Absolute value less than 3: −2, −1, 0, 1, 2.

A diver is 18 m below the surface of the water, and a bird flies 12 m above it. How big is the difference in height?

From −18 m to 12 m: 30 m.

How many years lie between 1 January 10 BC and 1 January AD 10? Careful: the year 1 BC is followed straight away by the year AD 1; there is no year 0.

On the number line it would be exactly 20 from −10 to 10. Because the year 0 is missing, it is 19 years.

2Number ranges and four quadrants

First you got to know the natural numbers, then the fractions. Now the negative numbers are added. Each new range contains the old one. You draw this as sets lying inside each other.

$\mathbb{N}$ are the natural numbers 0, 1, 2, … With the negative whole numbers you get the integers $\mathbb{Z}$: …, −2, −1, 0, 1, 2, … The fractions without a minus sign are called $\mathbb{Q}^+$. All fractions with and without a minus sign together are the rational numbers $\mathbb{Q}$.

The coordinate system gets bigger too: the x-axis continues to the left, the y-axis downwards. The axes divide the plane into four quadrants, numbered anticlockwise.

KEY POINT · NUMBER RANGES AND QUADRANTS

$\mathbb{N} \subset \mathbb{Z} \subset \mathbb{Q}$   ·   $\mathbb{N} \subset \mathbb{Q}^+ \subset \mathbb{Q}$

Point $P(x, y)$: first x (right/left), then y (up/down)

Quadrants: I: $x > 0,\, y > 0$ · II: $x < 0,\, y > 0$ · III: $x < 0,\, y < 0$ · IV: $x > 0,\, y < 0$

Symbol: $\subset$ means “is a subset of”. Every natural number is also an integer, but not the other way round.

Memory aid: you count the quadrants like the hands of a clock – only backwards.

INTERACTIVE · WHERE DOES THE NUMBER BELONG?

Assign each number to the smallest range it fits. Simplify first: $\tfrac{12}{4}$ is 3.

INTERACTIVE · FOUR QUADRANTS

Drag the point P and reflect it in an axis or in the origin. Which coordinate changes its sign?

EXAMPLE 3 · NUMBER RANGES

In which ranges does a) $-7$   b) $\tfrac{3}{5}$   c) $-0.25$   d) $9$ lie?

a) $\mathbb{Z}$ and $\mathbb{Q}$   b) $\mathbb{Q}^+$ and $\mathbb{Q}$   c) only $\mathbb{Q}$   d) in all four

every number lies in $\mathbb{Q}$

EXAMPLE 4 · REFLECTING

Reflect $P(3, -2)$ in the y-axis. In which quadrant does the image point lie?

Reflecting in the y-axis changes the sign of x: $P'(-3, -2)$.

quadrant III

EXERCISES

True or false? a) −3 is a natural number.   b) 0.5 is a rational number.   c) Every integer is a rational number.   d) $-\tfrac{8}{2}$ is an integer.

a) false   b) true   c) true   d) true, $-\tfrac82 = -4$

In which quadrant do $A(-2, 5)$, $B(4, -1)$, $C(-3, -3)$, $D(0, 2)$ lie?

A: II · B: IV · C: III · D: on the y-axis, in no quadrant

Draw the quadrilateral $A(-3, -2)$, $B(3, -2)$, $C(3, 2)$, $D(-3, 2)$. Which shape is it? How big are the perimeter and the area (1 unit = 1 cm)?

A rectangle of 6 cm and 4 cm: perimeter 20 cm, area 24 cm².

Reflect $Q(-4, 1)$ a) in the x-axis   b) in the y-axis   c) in the origin.

a) $(-4, -1)$   b) $(4, 1)$   c) $(4, -1)$

Three vertices of a square are $A(-1, -1)$, $B(2, -1)$, $C(2, 2)$. Find the fourth vertex. Does the centre of the square lie in a quadrant?

$D(-1, 2)$. Centre $(0.5, 0.5)$ – in quadrant I.

REVIEW · DEEPEN · CONNECT

A lift goes from the 3rd basement level (−3) to the 5th floor. How many floors does it travel?

From −3 to 0 is 3, from 0 to 5 another 5: 8 floors.

Give three rational numbers that lie between −1 and −0.9.

For example −0.95; −0.99; −0.91. Between two rational numbers there are always infinitely many more.

For which integers $a$ do $|a| < 4$ and $a < -1$ hold?

$|a| < 4$: −3, …, 3. Of these, less than −1: −3 and −2.

EXCURSIONHISTORY

Red and black rods

In Europe, negative numbers were rejected for a long time: as late as 1544 the German master of arithmetic Michael Stifel called them “absurd numbers”. In China people calculated with them much earlier.

The Chinese arithmetic book “The Nine Chapters on the Mathematical Art” was written about 2000 years ago. When solving systems of equations, the calculators laid rods on a board: red rods for gains, black ones for debts. The book also gives rules for adding and subtracting such numbers.

In the year 628 the Indian mathematician Brahmagupta wrote down rules for “fortunes” and “debts”, among them: a debt times a debt gives a fortune. That is the rule “minus times minus gives plus”, which you will meet in the next chapter.

Sources: “Jiuzhang suanshu” (Nine Chapters), chapter 8; Brahmagupta, “Brahmasphutasiddhanta”, 628; Michael Stifel, “Arithmetica integra”, Nuremberg 1544; after K. Shen, J. Crossley, A. Lun, “The Nine Chapters on the Mathematical Art”, Oxford 1999.
